info.bio:
Kate Bush (nacida Catherine Bush el 30 de julio de 1958 en Bexleyheath, Kent, ahora parte del Gran Londres) es una cantante y compositora británica. Tiene una voz expresiva, capaz de alcanzar un rango de tres octavas, y un estilo productivo ecléctico y meticulosamente musical. Debutó en 1978 con el single Wuthering Heights, que fue número uno en las listas musicales británicas durante cuatro semanas.

scenes.desc: La emancipación definitiva de la mujer en el rock (Terry Garthwaite, Joan Armatrading, Nanci Griffith y, sobre todo, Rickie Lee Jones, protegida de Tom Waits); la escuela tejana de cantautores herederos de Townes Van Zandt (Guy Clark, Butch Hancock, Joe Ely, Terry Allen, Rodney Crowell, T-Bone Burnett); el populismo melancólico de la posguerra de Vietnam (Warren Zevon, Rick Danko, Steve Forbert, John Hiatt, John Mellencamp, Don Henley, Donald Fagen, Robbie Robertson); y el puente de 1977 hacia la new wave: Peter Gabriel, poeta atormentado de las neurosis postindustriales, Marianne Faithfull y Kate Bush.

podcast.title: Early Retirement from Touring (1979)
podcast.body: Kate Bush famously retired from extensive touring in 1979 at the age of 20, after releasing only two albums. Her decision was influenced by the exhausting nature of touring and, significantly, by the tragic death of her lighting director in a fall during a warm-up show for "The Tour of Life." "First, she found the whole ordeal exhausting. Second, during a warm-up show for that road trip, which was called The Tour of Life, her lighting director was killed in a fall. And that really soured things."

podcast.title: Early Users of Fairlight CMI (1979 onwards)
podcast.body: Kate Bush was one of the artists who found "new possibilities" in the Fairlight CMI, a groundbreaking digital sampler released in 1979. Its ability to grab and manipulate audio bits allowed for innovative sound design in her work. "Peter Gabriel, Kate Bush, Brian Eno, David Byrne, New Order, and Thomas Dolby all saw new possibilities in the technology."

podcast.title: First Alternative Album Grammy Nominee (1991)
podcast.body: Kate Bush was among the initial nominees for the "Alternative Album" Grammy category when it was first introduced in 1991. This marked a significant step in the formal recognition of alternative music by the Recording Academy. "The first nominees were Kate Bush, the replacements, World Party, and Laurie Anderson."

podcast.title: Historic London Residency (2014)
podcast.body: After decades of minimal live appearances, Kate Bush announced a surprise 22-show residency at the Apollo Hammersmith in London in March 2014. Titled "Before the Dawn," the concerts, running from August 26th to October 1st, sold out within minutes and featured elaborate multimedia events with costumes, magicians, dancers, puppets, and 3D animation. "That is until March 2014 when she announced a 22-show residency at the Apollo Hammersmith in London. It began on August 26th and ended on October 1st."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: London Hammersmith Apollo Residency (2014)
podcast.body: Kate Bush returned to the stage for a 22-night residency at the London Hammersmith Apollo, starting in late August 2014, marking 35 years since her first tour. "It wasn't until she agreed to perform a 22-night residency at the London Hammersmith Apollo, starting in late August 2014, 35 years after that first tour, that she returned to the stage."

podcast.title: Alternative Artist on Major Label
podcast.body: Kate Bush was mentioned as an artist producing "delicate music" that was considered "alternative," despite recording for major labels. This illustrates the evolving and sometimes inconsistent application of the "alternative" label, which was not exclusively tied to artists on independent labels. "But the word was also used to describe delicate music from artists like Kate Bush or Tori Amos, both of whom, by the way, recorded from major labels."

podcast.title: Discovery by David Gilmour
podcast.body: At 14 years old, Kate Bush was discovered by David Gilmour of Pink Floyd, who chanced upon her playing piano, violin, organ, and writing her own songs. Recognizing her unique talent, Gilmour took her demo tape to EMI Records, leading to her signing. "David Gilmore of Pink Floyd, chanced upon a 14-year-old girl who had been playing piano, violin, and organ as well as writing her own songs."

podcast.body: At the age of 14, Kate Bush was discovered by David Gilmour of Pink Floyd. He immediately recognized her distinct talent, as she was already playing piano, violin, and organ, and writing her own songs. Gilmour took her demo tape to EMI Records, Pink Floyd's label. podcast.title: Diverse Musical Influences
podcast.body: Kate Bush's distinctive style is characterized by a wide array of musical influences. Fans have consistently identified elements of classical music, glam rock, folk music, and various wide-ranging ethnic music forms in her compositions. "For the years, fans were able to pick out the various influences in Kate's style, classical for sure. But there was also some glam rock in there, folk music, and also bits of wide-ranging ethnic music."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.body: Kate Bush is mentioned as an artist whose music, if dreamy, atmospheric, and immersive, could fit into the Dreampop scene of the late 80s to mid-90s.

podcast.title: EMI Records Deal and Artistic Development
podcast.body: EMI Records, seeking artists who sounded and looked different in the then-hot UK prog rock market, quickly signed Kate Bush to a deal. This arrangement allowed her to continue her schooling while developing as a musician. Over the next couple of years, she wrote more than 200 songs and performed in various pubs around London. "EMI quickly signed her to a deal that allowed her to continue to go to school and develop as a musician."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Early Career Development
podcast.body: EMI Records signed Kate Bush to a deal that allowed her to continue her schooling while developing her musical talents. Over the next few years, she wrote more than 200 songs and performed in various pubs across London, preparing her for her debut. "EMI quickly signed her to a deal that allowed her to continue to go to school and develop as a musician."

podcast.title: Early Development and Band
podcast.body: After being assigned to a record label, Kate Bush was allowed to mature and develop for a few years, spending part of that time playing with her family in an old farmhouse and performing in pubs at age 18 with a group called the KT Bushband. "She was assigned to a record label who then let her mature and develop for a few years while she played with her family in an old farmhouse. Part of that time was spent playing pubs when she was 18 with a group called the KT Bushband."

podcast.title: Early Musical Development and Discovery
podcast.body: Kate Bush began teaching herself piano at age 11, and by age 15, she was discovered by Pink Floyd's David Gilmour, a family friend. At this point, she also played violin and organ and had started writing her own songs, leading to a 50-track demo and a subsequent signing with EMI, coincidentally Pink Floyd's label. "Starting at the piano at age 11, she taught herself, she was discovered by Pink Floyd's David Gilmore when she was 15."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Family Background and Relationships
podcast.body: Kate Bush was raised Catholic, with her father being a doctor and her mother a nurse; she has two older brothers. Her first long-term relationship was with Dell Palmer, a bass player and recording engineer, which ended in the early 1990s. She is now married to guitarist Danny McIntosh and they have a son named Bertie. "We know a few things about Kate's personal life. Her family was well off with dad being a doctor and mum and nurse. She was raised Catholic as two older brothers. Her first long-term relationship was with Dell Palmer, a bass player and recording engineer, that ended in the early 1990s. She's now married to guitarist Danny McIntosh, and they have a son named Bertie."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Fanbase Loyalty and Respect for Privacy
podcast.body: Her fanbase maintains an insatiable thirst for her work while being very protective of their "quirky oddball goddess," with few celebrities having their privacy so well respected by their fans. "Kate Bush's sightings were like spotting the Loch Ness monster. Meanwhile, her fan base had both an insatiable thirst for her work, as well as being very protective of their quirky oddball goddess. Few celebrities have had their privacy so well respected by their fans."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Global Appeal and Critical Acclaim of Residency
podcast.body: Fans traveled from around the world to witness Kate Bush's "Before the Dawn" residency, a rare two-act, 25-song event. Reviews were overwhelmingly positive, and attendees left highly satisfied, despite the artist's subsequent return to not performing live shows. "People flew in from around the world to see a two-act event, plus encore, if you drink 25 songs."

podcast.title: Image as Reclusive Pop Star
podcast.body: Over the decades, Kate Bush has been portrayed as a reclusive pop star who refuses to engage in the music industry's games, releasing albums only occasionally. "Over the decade, she's been portrayed as a reclusive pop star, someone who refuses to play any of the music industry games. Albums come around only occasionally."

podcast.title: Limited Music Video Production
podcast.body: Kate Bush produced only a few music videos throughout her career. This selective approach contrasted with the increasing pressure on artists to create a video for every single release during the music video's golden age. "Kate Bush only made a few."

podcast.title: Limited Touring Post-Debut
podcast.body: After her debut album and a subsequent second album supported by a six-week tour, Kate Bush ceased touring extensively, citing exhaustion, a fear of flying, or possible trauma from a roadie's death in an accident during one of her early concerts. "A second album followed and it was supported by a six-week tour. And then that was it. No more tours. Too exhausting, said Kate. Or maybe it was a fear of flying. Or maybe she was traumatized when whatever Rodeys was killed in an accident during one of those early concerts."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Live Performance Absence
podcast.body: After an initial tour, Kate Bush refused to play any live shows for 35 years, which contributed to an aura of mystery, myth, and legend around her. This sustained enigma, combined with her unique artistry, has resulted in one of the most loyal and fanatical fan bases in the world. "And because she refused to play any live shows for 35 years after one initial tour, she was surrounded by an aura of mystery and myth and legend."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Long Hiatus from Live Performances
podcast.body: After an initial tour, Kate Bush famously refrained from playing any live shows for 35 years. This decision contributed to an aura of mystery, myth, and legend surrounding her, captivating many and fostering one of the most loyal and fanatical fan bases globally. "because she refused to play any live shows for 35 years after one initial tour, she was surrounded by an aura of mystery and myth and legend."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Prioritizing Private Life and Family
podcast.body: Kate Bush moved from London to the countryside, first to Berkshire and then to a remote area on the coast near Devon. She insisted on taking her time with her music, always in private, prioritizing her family and personal life above all else. "She moved from London to the countryside, first to Berkshire, and then to a remote area on the coast near Devon. She insisted on taking her time with her music, always in private, and her family and personal life came first beyond everything else."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Prolific Songwriting and Rapid Rise
podcast.body: Following her signing to EMI, Kate Bush continued her prolific songwriting, creating another 200 demos. She began working on her first album in August 1977, and within months, she quickly rose to become one of the best-known female singers across the UK. "Another 200 demos followed. And in August 1977, she started working on her first album. Within months, Kate was one of the best-known female singers in all of the UK."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Rare Public Sightings (1980s-Early 2000s)
podcast.body: Throughout the 1980s, Kate Bush was extremely rare to find in public, with only a few charity events in 1982, 1986, 1987, and 2002, and appearances for her 1993 album "The Red Shoes," marking her presence. "But whatever the case, finding Kate Bush in the wild through the 1980s was extremely rare. There was a charity event in 1982 and another in 1986 and another in 1987. Then in 1993, she made a few appearances in support of her album The Red Shoes, which came with a short film that she introduced at Screenings. There was another charity event in 2002 before another long, long absence."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Reclusive Lifestyle
podcast.body: Kate Bush spends most of her time at her home in Southeast London, completely out of public view, with her reasons for absence from the spotlight never adequately explained. She made videos under very controlled circumstances. "Most of the time Kate spent at her home in Southeast London, completely out of public view, and say for a very rare interview, and the one or two times she showed up to accept some kind of life-some achievement award, that's been it. But the reasons for her absence from the spotlight have never been adequately explained. She made videos, but under very controlled circumstances."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Recording at Abbey Road Studios
podcast.body: Kate Bush is among the list of legendary artists and bands who have made albums at the historic Abbey Road Studios in London. "I mean, Beatles, Pink Floyd, Oasis, Blur, Muse, Kate Bush, DePeshmo, Iron Maiden, Queen, You Tube Michael Jackson, Glenn Miller. They all made albums there."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Stop Me If You've Heard This One Before

podcast.title: Recording at Air Lyndhurst Hall
podcast.body: Kate Bush was a client at Air Lyndhurst Hall, George Martin's studio in North London, known for its large, hexagonal Studio One, suitable for orchestral and choir recordings. "Clients have included you too, Adele, Kate Bush, Liam Gallagher, Coldplay Muse, and Mumford and Sons."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Unconventionality and Reception
podcast.body: Kate Bush's music, particularly her debut single "Wuthering Heights," was considered highly unusual even during the punk years due to her singing style, range, and the literary basis of her hit song. She was adored by those who appreciated her "ethereal quirkiness," consistently refusing to conform to conventional or traditional music practices. "Nothing Kate did was conventional or traditional."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Unique and Ethereal Style
podcast.body: Kate Bush's style, characterized by her distinct singing, vocal range, and the unconventional nature of her hit songs, was not universally understood but deeply appreciated by those who "got her." Her appeal was often described as "ethereal quirkiness." "Not everyone got Kate Bush, of course, but those who did love her for her, well, let's just call it her ethereal cuckiness."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Recording at Air Lyndhurst Hall
xref.body: Adele was a client at Air Lyndhurst Hall, George Martin's studio in North London, utilizing its large Studio One, a hexagonal space capable of accommodating an entire orchestra and choir. "Clients have included you too, Adele, Kate Bush, Liam Gallagher, Coldplay Muse, and Mumford and Sons."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Romantic Link to Kate Bush
xref.body: Dell Palmer and Kate Bush were romantically linked in real life for a considerable period. "And yes, they were romantically linked in real life for a long time."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Spiritual Successor to Kate Bush
xref.body: Early alt-rock fans, familiar with Kate Bush's style, readily embraced Tori Amos as her "spiritual successor" due to her similarly highly emotional, confessional, and powerful musical output. "Back in some old school alt-rock fans remembered Kate Bush and embraced Tori as her spiritual successor."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Studio Engineer and Video Appearance
xref.body: Beyond his role as bass player, Palmer worked as a studio engineer for several of Kate Bush's albums and made appearances in some of her music videos. "Here he'd work as a studio engineer for several of her albums and also appeared in a couple of her videos."
